source.title: Safety Alignment Should Made Be More Than Just A Few Attention Head
source.citation: Safety Alignment Should Made Be More…

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some figures are represented only as plots, without extractable numerical values.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures refusal-direction projections in attention-head outputs under jailbreak prompts, a different operationalization of whether attacks suppress the refusal signal. It does not ablate or add the residual-stream direction itself.
record.gate_note: The study uses the refusal direction to rank attention heads, then ablates heads and measures harmfulness. This is not the claimed projection of one direction out of every layer and position. The attack analysis compares direction-projected head scores under original and jailbreak prompts. AHD attack-success, utility, and over-refusal results concern head-dropout training, not training against direct ablation of the refusal direction.
record.test_reason: Using the Arditi refusal direction, the study projects attention-head outputs onto it and compares harmful prompts with their jailbreak versions (Fig. 4, 8–10). This is a different method aimed at V3's question: do attacks suppress the direction's signal? It does not ablate or add the residual-stream direction, so V1 and V2 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that safety relies on a few attention heads, identified by projection onto the refusal direction. Jailbreaks reduce these heads' influence. AHD head-dropout training spreads safety across heads, sharply cuts jailbreak harmfulness (near zero for three of four models), and largely keeps utility without raising over-refusal.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a refusal direction to rank attention heads by projected output, then masks selected head outputs; does not project the residual-stream direction out of every layer and position or add it back.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported attack projection comparisons use different harmful prompts for the four models. For Llama-2, Adaptive increases the score on Head16.15 even though the cumulative score decreases.

fits_no_version.finding: Before AHD, masking attention heads ranked by refusal-direction projection sharply raises harmfulness (Llama-3 gives harmful output after 50 heads). After AHD, the rise is more gradual. In Qwen, heavy ablation yields confused non-committal replies (36% at 150 heads).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety-relevant contributions to the refusal direction are concentrated in a small set of mid-to-upper-layer attention heads, and head-dropout fine-tuning spreads them out.

record.problems: The direction-projection comparisons are presented as figures without extractable numerical values or stated uncertainty. They use selected top heads and illustrative prompts, so they do not establish that the residual-stream direction itself is causally suppressed. The paper notes that some heavily ablated Qwen outputs become uncertain or incoherent. Its AHD utility fine-tuning uses a limited Alpaca utility anchor, a limitation the authors acknowledge.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Table 1 jailbreak harmfulness outcomes, Table 2 utility benchmarks, and Table 3 over-refusal rates are not rows because they evaluate AHD head-dropout training rather than direct manipulation of the refusal direction or the direction-projection measurement used for V3.

untested.parts: There is no causal test that suppressing the direction produces the jailbreak. Projections are measured only in top-8 head outputs, not in the residual stream. No training against direction ablation was done; AHD is head dropout. The direction is not re-analysed under jailbreaks after AHD.
No ablation or addition of the residual-stream direction; only heads ranked by the direction are masked.
Not tested. The direction is recomputed separately for each model and AHD variant.
AHD changes how ablation effects spread across heads, but the study does not test whether a single removable direction exists.

record.verdict_notes: Rows r9–r24 were upgraded from partial to observed because the text states the scores are consistently and significantly lower. The weakness lies in scope (single prompt, head subset, no numbers, no causal test), not in effect size. Table 1 AHD jailbreak results concern head dropout, not training against direction ablation, so they do not bear on V3's robustness clause. The original source (arXiv:2406.11717) is only cited and used as a tool here.

versions.untested_parts: No direct ablation or addition of the residual-stream refusal direction, and no test of preserving general abilities after that intervention.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration.

The study measures refusal-direction projections in selected head outputs under attacks, not direct suppression of the residual-stream direction or the causal effect of that suppression on refusal. AHD is not training against direct refusal-direction ablation.
No test of affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts of refusal.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
No cross-language, model-variant, or base-to-instruct transfer test of the direction.
AHD is tested as a training intervention, but the study does not test how training choices determine whether a removable refusal direction exists.

labels.label: supports
labels.condition: Llama-2-7B-Chat, Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen-7B-Chat and Qwen2-7B-Instruct, each on one illustrative harmful prompt, under SI-GCG, AutoDAN-GA/HGA and Adaptive attacks; top-8 head projections onto the refusal direction
labels.reason: Text states jailbreak prompts give lower cumulative projection scores (Fig 4), with similar results for other models (B.5). This is correlational, figure-only and one prompt per model. AHD head dropout is not training against direction ablation, so V3's second clause is untested.

relation.reason: Its own results (Figs 4, 8-10) bear on V3's claim that attacks suppress the direction.

tranche.reason: Sec. 3.4 uses the Arditi refusal direction with a different method (head-output projections) to ask whether jailbreaks suppress its signal. It has no residual-stream ablation or addition.

source_check.notes: Pack gave no [lN] id for the verdict, so l1 is used. Appendix figure text is garbled; the prompt mapping for Qwen/Qwen-2 is inferred from text order and head IDs. The score is an unsigned magnitude |O_h·r|/||r||. Pack title is garbled: the text title is 'Safety Alignment Should Be Made More Than Just A Few Attention Heads' (arXiv:2508.19697v1).

statements.correction: 2508.19697: arXiv preprint v1 (27 Aug 2025), no venue in text (record class: preprint). No controls. Capability check: Table 2 utility benchmarks. ± uncertainty only in the AHD Tables 1-2, not in projection Figs 4, 8-10. Score is |O_h·r|/||r|| at the last prompt token, one prompt per model.
statements.problem: The finding for 2508.19697 is right, but the why-clause calls it peer-reviewed (ICASSP) with controls. The text is an arXiv preprint naming no venue, and it has no control condition.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: The four evaluated models and the illustrated SI-GCG, AutoDAN-GA, AutoDAN-HGA, and Adaptive jailbreak prompts
reader_labels.reason: The reported cumulative projections onto the refusal direction are lower for jailbreak prompts than for original harmful prompts, consistent with reduced safety-head influence (r9–r24). This is a projection-based association, not a direct causal test of direction suppression.
